145	**[6.1 Domain 1 --- Technical Security Measures (Commitments 1--9)]{.underline}**
146	
147	The following Commitments arise from the Commissioner\'s findings, as detailed in Schedule 1 (Findings 1--5), regarding BHS UK\'s failure to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, contrary to Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner found that the technical security posture of the BellCloud UK environment was materially deficient in several respects, and that these deficiencies directly contributed to the occurrence and severity of the Breach.
148	
149	**Commitment 1 --- Automated Patch Management.** BHS UK shall implement an automated patch management system across the entire BellCloud UK infrastructure, including all operating systems, middleware, application components, API gateways, database management systems, and third-party libraries. The automated patch management system shall ensure that:
150	
151	> \(a\) all critical and high-severity vulnerabilities (as classified by CVSS score of 7.0 or above, or by vendor classification, whichever results in the higher severity classification) are patched within a maximum of fourteen (14) calendar days from the date of public disclosure of the vulnerability;
152	>
153	> \(b\) medium-severity vulnerabilities (CVSS score of 4.0 to 6.9) are patched within thirty (30) calendar days from the date of public disclosure;
154	>
155	> \(c\) the system provides real-time reporting and dashboarding on patch compliance status across all components, viewable by the DPO and IT security management; and
156	>
157	> \(d\) patch compliance is reviewed by the DPO on a monthly basis, with documented sign-off and escalation of any non-compliant items to the Managing Director.
158	
159	BHS UK acknowledges that the fourteen-day patching cycle for critical vulnerabilities reflects the minimum standard expected by the Commissioner in light of the circumstances of the Breach, where a thirty-four-day patching gap for a critical vulnerability directly enabled the unauthorised access.
160	
161	**Commitment 2 --- Encryption Standards.** BHS UK shall implement the following encryption standards across the BellCloud UK environment:
162	
163	> \(a\) encryption at rest using Advanced Encryption Standard with 256-bit keys (\"AES-256\") for all personal data stores within BellCloud UK and any associated storage systems, including databases, file stores, backup media, and archive storage; and
164	>
165	> \(b\) encryption in transit using Transport Layer Security version 1.3 (\"TLS 1.3\") for all data flows to, from, and within BellCloud UK, including all connections with NHS trusts, private clinics, any third-party systems, and all internal service-to-service communications. No fallback to lower protocol versions (including TLS 1.2, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0, or any earlier version) shall be permitted. BHS UK shall disable all cipher suites associated with protocol versions lower than TLS 1.3 on all endpoints within the BellCloud UK environment.
166	
167	BHS UK shall maintain documentation of all encryption configurations and shall ensure that encryption key management procedures are in place in accordance with industry best practice, including secure key generation, storage, rotation, and destruction.
168	
169	**Commitment 3 --- Access Controls.** BHS UK shall implement a comprehensive access control overhaul across all systems processing personal data within the BellCloud UK environment, including:
170	
171	> \(a\) role-based access control (\"RBAC\") across all systems processing personal data, with roles defined in accordance with the principle of least privilege and mapped to specific job functions;
172	>
173	> \(b\) enforcement of the principle of least privilege through automated provisioning, ensuring that each user account has access only to the minimum data and system functions necessary for the user\'s specific role;
174	>
175	> \(c\) quarterly access reviews with documented sign-off by the responsible line manager and the DPO, including verification that all access rights remain appropriate and proportionate; and
176	>
177	> \(d\) immediate revocation procedures for leavers and role-changers, with access revoked within four (4) hours of the effective date of departure or role change, enforced through integration with human resources systems.
178	
179	**Commitment 4 --- Network Segmentation.** BHS UK shall implement network segmentation of the BellCloud UK environment to isolate:
180	
181	> \(a\) patient data processing zones from corporate IT networks, ensuring that no direct network path exists between corporate workstations and patient data stores;
182	>
183	> \(b\) production environments from Non-Production Environments, ensuring that Non-Production Environments cannot access production data stores and that data flows between production and Non-Production Environments are controlled and logged;
184	>
185	> \(c\) each NHS trust\'s data from other trusts\' data through logical separation, ensuring that no trust can access another trust\'s data through the application or at the infrastructure level; and
186	>
187	> \(d\) administrative access pathways from data access pathways, ensuring that system administration functions are accessible only through dedicated, hardened management interfaces.
188	
189	**Commitment 5 --- API Security.** BHS UK shall implement a comprehensive API security programme including:
190	
191	> \(a\) deployment of an API gateway with rate limiting, authentication, input validation, and schema enforcement for all external-facing APIs within the BellCloud UK environment;
192	>
193	> \(b\) regular API security testing, conducted no less than quarterly, using automated tools and manual review;
194	>
195	> \(c\) maintenance of a complete API inventory documenting all endpoints, including their purpose, authentication requirements, data exposure, and risk classification; and
196	>
197	> \(d\) deprecation and decommissioning of any legacy API endpoints not meeting current security standards within thirty (30) days of identification.
198	
199	**Commitment 6 --- Penetration Testing.** BHS UK shall engage an independent CREST-accredited penetration testing provider to conduct external penetration testing of the BellCloud UK environment on a quarterly basis, such that no fewer than four (4) penetration tests are conducted in each calendar year. The penetration testing provider shall be independent of BHS UK and shall not be a firm that has provided forensic investigation, remediation consulting, or other cybersecurity services to BHS UK in connection with the Breach. For the avoidance of doubt, this requirement precludes the engagement of Ridgeline Cybersecurity Consultants Ltd. for the purposes of penetration testing under this Commitment. All findings rated critical or high severity must be remediated within thirty (30) days of the date of the test report. The full penetration test reports shall be made available to the Commissioner upon request.
200	
201	**Commitment 7 --- Vulnerability Scanning.** BHS UK shall implement continuous automated vulnerability scanning across all internet-facing and internal systems within the BellCloud UK environment, with:
202	
203	> \(a\) scans conducted no less frequently than weekly across all in-scope systems;
204	>
205	> \(b\) results triaged by qualified personnel within forty-eight (48) hours of scan completion; and
206	>
207	> \(c\) a documented remediation workflow integrated with the automated patch management system required by Commitment 1, ensuring that vulnerabilities identified through scanning are tracked through to resolution.
208	
209	**Commitment 8 --- Logging and Monitoring.** BHS UK shall implement a centralised logging and security information and event management (\"SIEM\") system that:
210	
211	> \(a\) captures all access events, authentication events (including successful and failed login attempts), data exports, administrative actions, configuration changes, and privilege escalations across all systems within the BellCloud UK environment;
212	>
213	> \(b\) retains logs for a minimum of twelve (12) months in a tamper-evident, immutable log store;
214	>
215	> \(c\) provides real-time alerting for anomalous activity, including unusual data access patterns, high-volume data exports, access from unusual locations, and repeated failed authentication attempts; and
216	>
217	> \(d\) is monitored by qualified security personnel on a 24-hours-per-day, 7-days-per-week basis, either through in-house security operations or through a managed security operations centre (\"SOC\") provided by a suitably qualified third party.
218	
219	**Commitment 9 --- Multi-Factor Authentication.** BHS UK shall implement multi-factor authentication (\"MFA\") for:
220	
221	> \(a\) all administrative access to BellCloud UK systems, including infrastructure, platform, and application administration;
222	>
223	> \(b\) all remote access by BHS UK staff, whether via virtual private network, remote desktop, or any other remote access mechanism;
224	>
225	> \(c\) all access to systems containing special category data, regardless of whether access is local or remote; and
226	>
227	> \(d\) all third-party access to BellCloud UK, including access by NHS trust and private clinic personnel through partner portals or APIs.
228	
229	MFA shall utilise at least two independent authentication factors from different categories (knowledge, possession, and inherence). SMS-based one-time passwords shall not be accepted as a sole second factor due to known vulnerabilities.
230	
231	**[6.2 Domain 2 --- Data Protection Impact Assessments (Commitments 10--14)]{.underline}**
232	
233	The following Commitments arise from the Commissioner\'s findings, as detailed in Schedule 1 (Findings 6 and 10), regarding BHS UK\'s failure to conduct adequate Data Protection Impact Assessments contrary to Articles 35 and 36 of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner found that BHS UK had not conducted a DPIA in respect of the BellCloud UK processing despite the processing involving large-scale processing of special category health data, which is a type of processing specifically identified in Article 35(3)(b) as requiring a DPIA.
234	
235	**Commitment 10 --- DPIA Framework.** BHS UK shall develop and implement a comprehensive DPIA framework that:
236	
237	> \(a\) establishes clear criteria for when a DPIA is required, aligned with Article 35 of the UK GDPR and the Commissioner\'s published guidance on DPIAs;
238	>
239	> \(b\) defines a standardised DPIA methodology and templates, ensuring consistency and completeness across all assessments;
240	>
241	> \(c\) requires DPO sign-off on all DPIAs prior to the commencement of any processing activity that is the subject of the DPIA; and
242	>
243	> \(d\) integrates DPIA requirements into project management and change control processes, ensuring that no new processing activity or significant change to existing processing can proceed without a DPIA screening assessment.
244	
245	**Commitment 11 --- Retrospective DPIAs.** BHS UK shall conduct retrospective DPIAs on all existing processing activities involving personal data within BellCloud UK, prioritising processing activities that involve special category data. All retrospective DPIAs shall be completed within one hundred and eighty (180) days of the Commencement Date. Each retrospective DPIA shall assess the necessity and proportionality of the processing, identify and assess risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, and identify measures to mitigate those risks.
246	
247	**Commitment 12 --- DPIA Review Triggers.** BHS UK shall define and implement documented DPIA review triggers including:
248	
249	> \(a\) any new processing activity involving personal data;
250	>
251	> \(b\) significant changes to existing processing activities, including changes to the purpose, scope, context, or technology of processing;
252	>
253	> \(c\) changes to the risk environment, including new threat intelligence, changes in the regulatory landscape, or the identification of new vulnerabilities; and
254	>
255	> \(d\) at minimum, annual review of all existing DPIAs to assess whether the risk profile of the processing has changed.
256	
257	**Commitment 13 --- ICO Consultation Threshold.** BHS UK shall establish a formal, documented process for consulting the Commissioner under Article 36 of the UK GDPR where a DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by BHS UK to mitigate the risk, and the residual risk remains high after the application of mitigating measures. BHS UK shall document all decisions regarding whether consultation with the Commissioner is required, including the reasoning for any decision not to consult, with DPO sign-off on all such decisions.
258	
259	**Commitment 14 --- DPIA Register.** BHS UK shall establish and maintain a central DPIA register, accessible to the DPO and to the Commissioner upon request, listing all completed DPIAs, their review dates, outcomes, residual risks accepted by senior management (with documented justification), and the date of the next scheduled review. The register shall be updated within five (5) business days of the completion or review of any DPIA.
260	
261	**[6.3 Domain 3 --- Data Processor Management (Commitments 15--20)]{.underline}**
262	
263	The following Commitments arise from the Commissioner\'s findings, as detailed in Schedule 1 (Findings 7, 8, 11, and 12), regarding BHS UK\'s failure to exercise adequate oversight of processors and sub-processors, and its failure to ensure that contractual arrangements with processors complied with Article 28 of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner found that several of BHS UK\'s data processing agreements were outdated and did not contain all mandatory provisions required by Article 28(3), and that BHS UK had no formal programme for monitoring sub-processor compliance.
264	
265	**Commitment 15 --- Processor Audit Programme.** BHS UK shall implement a formal processor audit programme under which all processors processing personal data on behalf of BHS UK are audited at least annually against data protection requirements. Audits shall assess compliance with the terms of the data processing agreement, technical and organisational security measures, sub-processor management, and data subject rights fulfilment. All audit reports shall be reviewed by the DPO, and any material non-compliance shall be escalated to the Managing Director and, where appropriate, to the board.
266	
267	**Commitment 16 --- Updated Article 28 Agreements.** BHS UK shall review and update all data processing agreements with processors to ensure full compliance with Article 28(3) of the UK GDPR, including all mandatory provisions specified therein, namely: (a) processing only on documented instructions; (b) confidentiality obligations; (c) security measures; (d) sub-processor conditions; (e) assistance with data subject rights; (f) assistance with breach notification and DPIAs; (g) deletion or return of data on termination; and (h) audit rights. All updated agreements shall be executed within the timeframe specified for this Commitment in Section 7.
268	
269	**Commitment 17 --- Sub-Processor Due Diligence.** BHS UK shall implement a formal sub-processor due diligence programme, to include:
270	
271	> \(a\) pre-engagement privacy risk assessments for all sub-processors, conducted before any sub-processor is permitted to process personal data;
272	>
273	> \(b\) annual compliance audits of all sub-processors, covering technical and organisational security measures, data protection practices, and compliance with the terms of the sub-processing agreement; and
274	>
275	> \(c\) contractual flow-down of all Article 28 obligations to sub-processors through the data processing chain, ensuring that each sub-processor is bound by the same data protection obligations as the processor.
276	
277	BHS UK shall maintain a register of all approved sub-processors, including the identity, location, and scope of processing of each sub-processor, and shall not permit any processor to engage a sub-processor without BHS UK\'s prior written authorisation. The sub-processor register shall be made available to the Commissioner upon request.
278	
279	**Commitment 18 --- Processor Breach Notification Chain.** BHS UK shall contractually require all processors and sub-processors to notify BHS UK of any personal data breach without undue delay and in any event within twenty-four (24) hours of the processor\'s or sub-processor\'s discovery of the breach. BHS UK shall establish a documented notification chain from processor to BHS UK\'s DPO, ensuring that all breach notifications received from processors are immediately triaged and assessed. The contractual requirement shall specify the minimum content of breach notifications, including the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate number of data subjects affected, and the measures taken to contain and remediate the breach.
280	
281	**Commitment 19 --- Processor Data Return/Deletion.** BHS UK shall contractually require all processors to return or securely delete all personal data upon termination of the processing relationship, with written certification of deletion provided to BHS UK, in accordance with Article 28(3)(g) of the UK GDPR. BHS UK shall verify compliance with this requirement through its processor audit programme (Commitment 15) and shall retain evidence of deletion certifications for the duration of this Undertaking and for a period of two (2) years thereafter.
282	
283	**Commitment 20 --- International Transfer Safeguards.** BHS UK shall implement appropriate safeguards for all international transfers of personal data to countries or territories outside the United Kingdom that are not subject to an adequacy decision by the Secretary of State. Appropriate safeguards shall include, as applicable, Standard Contractual Clauses adopted pursuant to Section 119A of the Data Protection Act 2018 and Transfer Risk Assessments conducted in compliance with Chapter V of the UK GDPR and the Commissioner\'s published guidance on international data transfers. This obligation applies to all transfers outside the United Kingdom, including but not limited to transfers to processors, sub-processors, and any entities within the BHS corporate group (including, without limitation, any transfers to BHS Inc. in the United States of America). BHS UK shall maintain a register of all international transfers and shall document the safeguards applied to each transfer.
284	
285	**[6.4 Domain 4 --- Staff Training & Awareness (Commitments 21--26)]{.underline}**
286	
287	The following Commitments arise from the Commissioner\'s findings, as detailed in Schedule 1 (Finding 9), regarding insufficient staff awareness and training on data protection matters. The Commissioner found that BHS UK\'s last mandatory data protection training for all staff had been conducted approximately eighteen (18) months prior to the Breach, and that no role-based specialist training had been provided to staff in high-risk data processing roles.
288	
289	**Commitment 21 --- Mandatory Annual Training.** BHS UK shall ensure that all UK staff (currently 342 employees, and any additional staff employed during the term of this Undertaking) complete mandatory annual data protection training. Training shall be delivered by a qualified external training provider, selected by BHS UK and approved by the DPO. The training shall include assessed competency verification for each participant, to confirm that the participant has attained an adequate understanding of the material covered. Training shall cover, at minimum:
290	
291	> \(a\) UK GDPR principles and their application to BHS UK\'s processing activities;
292	>
293	> \(b\) data subject rights and BHS UK\'s obligations in respect of those rights;
294	>
295	> \(c\) breach identification and reporting, including the internal escalation SLA required by Commitment 33;
296	>
297	> \(d\) special category data handling and the additional protections required;
298	>
299	> \(e\) role-relevant data protection obligations, tailored to the participant\'s specific function within BHS UK; and
300	>
301	> \(f\) the obligations arising under this Undertaking, to the extent relevant to the participant\'s role.
302	
303	New joiners shall complete mandatory training within thirty (30) days of their start date. All training records, including attendance, assessment scores, and completion dates, shall be maintained for the duration of this Undertaking.
304	
305	**Commitment 22 --- Role-Based Specialist Training.** BHS UK shall implement role-based specialist training for staff in high-risk data processing roles, including but not limited to IT security, software development, clinical data management, customer support, and data analytics functions. Specialist training shall be delivered at least annually and shall address the specific data protection risks and obligations relevant to each role. The DPO shall approve the content and scope of all specialist training programmes.
306	
307	**Commitment 23 --- Phishing Simulation.** BHS UK shall implement a phishing simulation programme with simulated phishing attacks conducted no less than quarterly across all staff. Results shall be tracked at the individual and team level, and targeted remedial training shall be provided to any staff member who fails a simulation. Aggregate results shall be reported to the DPO and included in quarterly board reports (Commitment 25).
308	
309	**Commitment 24 --- Training Completion KPIs.** BHS UK shall establish and monitor training completion key performance indicators (\"KPIs\") requiring:
310	
311	> \(a\) 100% completion of mandatory annual training within thirty (30) days of each annual training cycle;
312	>
313	> \(b\) a 95% pass rate on competency assessments, with additional training provided to staff who do not achieve a pass; and
314	>
315	> \(c\) disciplinary escalation for non-completion of mandatory training, in accordance with BHS UK\'s staff disciplinary procedures.
316	
317	**Commitment 25 --- Board-Level Reporting on Training.** BHS UK shall include data protection training metrics in its quarterly board reports, including training completion rates, competency assessment scores, phishing simulation results, and any remedial actions taken. The DPO shall present training metrics as a standing item at each board meeting.
318	
319	**Commitment 26 --- DPO Resource Allocation.** BHS UK shall ensure that the DPO has adequate resources, including a dedicated privacy team of no fewer than four (4) full-time equivalent staff, to discharge the DPO\'s duties effectively under Article 38 of the UK GDPR. BHS UK shall not reduce the DPO\'s resources during the term of this Undertaking without the prior written approval of the Commissioner. The DPO\'s budget allocation shall be reported to the board on a quarterly basis.
320	
321	**[6.5 Domain 5 --- Data Minimisation & Retention (Commitments 27--31)]{.underline}**
322	
323	The following Commitments arise from the Commissioner\'s findings regarding BHS UK\'s failure to comply with the data minimisation principle under Article 5(1)(c) and the storage limitation principle under Article 5(1)(e) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner found that BHS UK retained personal data, including special category health data, beyond periods that could be justified by reference to the purposes for which the data was processed, and that copies of production data containing real patient records were used in Non-Production Environments without adequate safeguards.
324	
325	**Commitment 27 --- Retention Schedule Overhaul.** BHS UK shall overhaul its data retention schedule to define lawful retention periods for all categories of personal data processed within the BellCloud UK environment and across BHS UK\'s operations. Each retention period shall be supported by documented justification, identifying the legal basis for retention and the purpose or purposes for which the data is retained. The retention schedule shall be approved by the DPO and reviewed at least annually.
326	
327	**Commitment 28 --- Automated Deletion Workflows.** BHS UK shall implement automated deletion workflows to ensure that personal data is securely deleted upon expiry of the applicable retention period defined in the retention schedule (Commitment 27). Each deletion event shall be logged with confirmation of deletion, including the category of data deleted, the retention period that expired, the date of deletion, and the method of deletion. The DPO shall receive monthly reports on automated deletion activity.
328	
329	**Commitment 29 --- Pseudonymisation Roadmap.** BHS UK shall develop and implement a pseudonymisation roadmap with the following elements:
330	
331	> \(a\) defined technical standards specifying the pseudonymisation methodology to be used, including the technical processes for separating identifiers from content data and the safeguards applied to the re-identification key;
332	>
333	> \(b\) implementation milestones at sixty (60), one hundred and twenty (120), and one hundred and eighty (180) days from the Commencement Date, with documented progress at each milestone; and
334	>
335	> \(c\) coverage targets ensuring that one hundred percent (100%) of special category health data is pseudonymised in all Non-Production Environments within one hundred and eighty (180) days of the Commencement Date.
336	
337	For the avoidance of doubt, \"Non-Production Environments\" includes all testing, development, staging, quality assurance, analytics, and reporting environments, as defined in Clause 3.1 of this Undertaking. 354	**[Schedule 1: Summary of Commissioner\'s Findings]{.underline}**
355	
356	**ICO Case Reference: ICO/INV/2024/09871**
357	
358	The following is a summary of the fourteen (14) specific failings identified by the Commissioner during the investigation into the Breach and BHS UK\'s data protection practices. These findings are referenced in the Recitals (Clause 2.5) and form the basis for the Commitments set out in Section 6 of the Undertaking.
359	
360	**[Technical Failings (Findings 1--5)]{.underline}**
361	
362	**Finding 1 --- Failure to Patch CVE-2024-31742 Within a Reasonable Timeframe.** BHS UK failed to apply the available security patch for vulnerability CVE-2024-31742 within a reasonable timeframe following its public disclosure. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 14 August 2024 with a critical CVSS score and an available vendor patch. BHS UK did not apply the patch before the Breach on 17 September 2024, a period of thirty-four (34) calendar days. The Commissioner considers that a reasonable timeframe for patching a critical vulnerability of this nature, particularly in a system processing special category health data at scale, would have been no more than fourteen (14) calendar days. BHS UK\'s patch management processes at the time of the Breach were manual and ad hoc, with no automated tracking of vulnerability disclosures or patch availability. This failing contravenes Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR.
363	
364	**Finding 2 --- Inadequate Encryption Standards for Data in Transit.** The Commissioner\'s investigation identified that certain connections within the BellCloud UK environment, including connections with a number of NHS trusts and private clinics, were using Transport Layer Security versions 1.0 and 1.1, which are known to contain security vulnerabilities and which have been deprecated by industry standards bodies. The use of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 for the transmission of personal data, and in particular special category health data, is not consistent with the obligation to implement appropriate technical measures under Article 32(1)(a) of the UK GDPR.
365	
366	**Finding 3 --- Lack of Network Segmentation Between Production and Non-Production Environments.** The Commissioner found that the BellCloud UK production environment was not adequately segmented from Non-Production Environments. In particular, development and testing environments shared network infrastructure with the production environment, and copies of production data containing real patient records were accessible within development and testing environments. This configuration increased the attack surface and the potential impact of any compromise, contrary to Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 of the UK GDPR.
367	
368	**Finding 4 --- Absence of Multi-Factor Authentication for Administrative Access.** The Commissioner found that multi-factor authentication was not required for administrative access to BellCloud UK systems. Administrative accounts with elevated privileges, capable of accessing patient data and modifying system configurations, were protected only by single-factor password authentication. The absence of MFA for administrative access represents a significant security deficiency, particularly given the volume and sensitivity of the personal data processed, contrary to Article 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR.
369	
370	**Finding 5 --- Insufficient Logging and Monitoring.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK did not operate a security information and event management (\"SIEM\") system, and that system logs were retained for only thirty (30) days. The absence of a SIEM system meant that BHS UK had limited ability to detect anomalous activity in real time, and the short log retention period meant that forensic investigation of the Breach was hampered. The Commissioner considers that a minimum of twelve (12) months\' log retention is appropriate for a system processing personal data of this nature and at this scale, contrary to Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR.
371	
372	**[Organisational Failings (Findings 6--9)]{.underline}**
373	
374	**Finding 6 --- No Comprehensive DPIA Conducted for BellCloud UK Processing.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK had not conducted a Data Protection Impact Assessment in respect of the BellCloud UK processing, despite the processing involving large-scale processing of special category health data for 47 NHS trusts and 218 private clinics. Such processing falls squarely within Article 35(3)(b) of the UK GDPR (processing on a large scale of special categories of data), which requires a DPIA to be carried out. This failing contravenes Article 35 of the UK GDPR.
375	
376	**Finding 7 --- Outdated Data Processing Agreements Not Compliant with Article 28(3).** The Commissioner found that several of BHS UK\'s data processing agreements with processors were outdated and did not contain all of the mandatory provisions required by Article 28(3) of the UK GDPR. In particular, certain agreements lacked adequate provisions regarding sub-processing, audit rights, and data return and deletion obligations. This failing contravenes Article 28 of the UK GDPR.
377	
378	**Finding 8 --- No Formal Sub-Processor Oversight Programme.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK had no formal programme for overseeing sub-processors engaged by its processors. BHS UK was unable to provide a complete list of sub-processors processing personal data on its behalf, and had not conducted any due diligence or compliance audits of sub-processors. This failing contravenes Article 28(2) of the UK GDPR.
379	
380	**Finding 9 --- Inadequate Staff Training.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK\'s last mandatory data protection training for all staff had been conducted approximately eighteen (18) months prior to the Breach. No role-based specialist training had been provided to staff in high-risk data processing roles (including IT security and software development). The Commissioner considers that annual mandatory training, supplemented by role-based specialist training, represents the minimum standard for an organisation processing special category health data at this scale. This failing contravenes Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR.
381	
382	**[DPIA/Processor Failings (Findings 10--12)]{.underline}**
383	
384	**Finding 10 --- No DPIA Register Maintained.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK did not maintain a central register of DPIAs, and was unable to demonstrate that DPIAs had been considered for any of its processing activities. The absence of a DPIA register indicates a systemic failure to embed DPIA processes into BHS UK\'s operations, contrary to Article 35 of the UK GDPR and the Commissioner\'s published guidance.
385	
386	**Finding 11 --- No Processor Audit Programme.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK had no formal processor audit programme. BHS UK was unable to demonstrate that it had audited any of its processors against data protection requirements in the three years prior to the Breach. This failing contravenes Articles 28(1) and 28(3)(h) of the UK GDPR, which require the controller to use only processors providing sufficient guarantees and to ensure that audit rights are exercised.
387	
388	**Finding 12 --- International Transfers Without Adequate Safeguards.** The Commissioner found that personal data was being transferred from BHS UK\'s UK operations to BHS Inc.\'s systems in the United States without adequate safeguards in place. Specifically, BHS UK had not conducted Transfer Risk Assessments and had not implemented Standard Contractual Clauses or any other appropriate safeguard under Chapter V of the UK GDPR in respect of certain intra-group data transfers. This failing contravenes Articles 44 to 49 of the UK GDPR.
389	
390	**[Breach Response Failings (Findings 13--14)]{.underline}**
391	
392	**Finding 13 --- Incident Response Plan Outdated and Not Tested.** The Commissioner found that BHS UK\'s incident response plan had last been updated in 2021, approximately three years prior to the Breach. The plan had not been tested through simulation exercises at any point since its adoption. The plan did not reflect BHS UK\'s current systems architecture, staff structure, or regulatory obligations. This failing contravenes Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR.
393	
394	**Finding 14 --- Excessive Internal Escalation Time.** The Commissioner found that internal escalation from the initial detection of the Breach by BHS UK\'s IT monitoring systems to notification of the DPO took approximately thirty-eight (38) hours. The initial detection occurred at approximately 02:15 on 17 September 2024, but the DPO was not notified until approximately 16:00 on 18 September 2024. The Commissioner considers that a thirty-eight-hour internal escalation time is excessive and could have jeopardised BHS UK\'s ability to notify the Commissioner within the seventy-two-hour timeframe required by Article 33(1) of the UK GDPR. An internal escalation SLA of no more than twenty-four (24) hours is appropriate for an organisation of BHS UK\'s size and the sensitivity of the data processed.
395	
396	**Note on Records Affected:** The Breach compromised a total of 312,417 patient records: 41,203 records containing mental health treatment data (special category data under Article 9); 87,614 records containing prescription data; and 183,600 records containing general medical data.
397	
398	**Note on Patching Delay:** The Commissioner notes a thirty-four (34) calendar day gap between the public disclosure of CVE-2024-31742 on 14 August 2024 and the exploitation of the vulnerability on 17 September 2024. A vendor patch was available from the date of disclosure. The Commissioner considers that this delay directly contributed to the occurrence of the Breach.

22	**[1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]{.underline}**
23	
24	Bellhaven Health Systems, Inc. (\"BHS\"), a Delaware corporation headquartered at 4200 Innovation Drive, Suite 800, Austin, TX 78759, operates in the United Kingdom through its wholly owned subsidiary Bellhaven Health UK Ltd. (\"BHS UK\"), a private limited company incorporated in England and Wales (Company No. 09847321), with its registered office at 15 Cavendish Square, London W1G 0BA. BHS develops and operates cloud-based electronic health record (\"EHR\") and telemedicine platforms serving healthcare providers across the United States, the United Kingdom, and selected international markets. In FY2024, BHS reported consolidated annual revenue of approximately USD 485 million, of which approximately GBP 62 million was attributable to UK operations. BHS UK processes personal data, including special category health data, on behalf of 47 NHS trusts and 218 private clinics across England, Scotland, and Wales through its proprietary BellCloud UK platform.
25	
26	On 17 September 2024, BHS UK\'s Security Operations Centre (\"SOC\") detected unauthorised access to the BellCloud UK patient data environment. Subsequent forensic investigation established that the breach was caused by the exploitation of CVE-2024-31742, a critical vulnerability in an API gateway component that had been publicly disclosed on 14 August 2024 --- thirty-four days prior to the breach. The incident resulted in the exfiltration of 312,417 UK patient records, comprising 41,203 mental health treatment records, 87,614 prescription data records, and 183,600 general medical records. The affected data included full patient names, NHS numbers, dates of birth, medical diagnoses (ICD-10 codes), and prescription histories. BHS UK notified the Information Commissioner\'s Office (\"ICO\") on 19 September 2024, within the statutory seventy-two-hour notification period, and data subject notifications were issued between 25 September and 12 October 2024.
27	
28	The ICO commenced a formal investigation on 2 October 2024 under Case Reference ICO/INV/2024/09871, led by Deputy Commissioner Eleanor Voss. Following the investigation, the ICO identified fourteen specific failings across technical measures, organisational measures, data protection impact assessment practices, processor oversight, and breach response. A Preliminary Enforcement Notice was issued on 18 November 2024. Following constructive engagement between BHS UK, the ICO, and Thornfield & Associates LLP, a Regulatory Undertaking was signed on 15 January 2025 by Jonathan Kierce, Managing Director of BHS UK, and Deputy Commissioner Voss, as an alternative to formal enforcement action. The Undertaking contains forty-seven specific commitments across eight domains, with phased implementation deadlines spanning twelve months.
29	
30	This Remediation Implementation Plan (the \"Plan\") provides a comprehensive and robust response to all forty-seven commitments contained in the Regulatory Undertaking. The Plan sets out fifty-two action items across eight workstreams, each mirroring a corresponding domain of the Undertaking. Certain commitments have been subdivided into discrete implementation sub-actions to ensure operational clarity and effective project tracking. Each action item has been assigned a designated owner, an allocated budget, a target completion date aligned with the relevant Undertaking phase, and defined evidence deliverables. The Plan is designed to demonstrate BHS UK\'s unequivocal commitment to achieving and maintaining full compliance with the UK General Data Protection Regulation (\"UK GDPR\") and the Data Protection Act 2018.
31	
32	The total remediation budget of GBP 4.2 million was approved by the BHS board of directors on 28 January 2025. BHS UK has engaged Ridgeline Cybersecurity Consultants Ltd. (lead consultant: Dr. Amir Kassab, CISSP, CISM) since 5 October 2024 to assist with forensic investigation and technical remediation activities. Pendleton Audit Group LLP (lead: Sarah Greenhalgh, CISA, CRISC) was appointed on 20 January 2025 as the independent auditor for compliance verification purposes. Cyber insurance coverage under the policy issued by Kestrel Underwriting Syndicate (policy no. KUS-CY-2024-0847), providing GBP 5 million per occurrence and GBP 10 million aggregate cover, is available to offset certain remediation and incident response costs, subject to policy terms and conditions.
33	
34	Key personnel with oversight of the remediation programme include: Marcus Ellingham, Chief Executive Officer of BHS; Priya Dasgupta, General Counsel of BHS; Dr. Fiona Hartwell, Data Protection Officer of BHS UK; and Jonathan Kierce, Managing Director of BHS UK. Thornfield & Associates LLP serves as external legal adviser to BHS UK in all matters relating to the Undertaking and this Plan.
35	
36	The Plan is organised into eight workstreams, with implementation phased across four periods aligned with the Undertaking milestones. The following sections provide a detailed description of each workstream, including action item specifications, accountability structures, budget allocations, and target dates for completion.
37	
38	**[2. BACKGROUND AND CONTEXT]{.underline}**
39	
40	**2.1 The Data Breach**
41	
42	On 17 September 2024, at approximately 02:47 GMT, BHS UK\'s Security Operations Centre detected anomalous data exfiltration patterns from the BellCloud UK patient data environment. Automated intrusion detection systems flagged a sustained outbound data transfer from a production database cluster hosting patient records for NHS trust clients and private clinic partners. Incident response procedures were initiated immediately, and the affected API gateway was isolated from the network within ninety minutes of initial detection.
43	
44	The subsequent forensic investigation, conducted by Ridgeline Cybersecurity Consultants Ltd. (engaged 5 October 2024, lead consultant: Dr. Amir Kassab, CISSP, CISM), established that the root cause of the breach was the exploitation of CVE-2024-31742, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the BellCloud UK API gateway component. This vulnerability had been publicly disclosed by the vendor on 14 August 2024, and a patch had been made available on the same date. BHS UK had not applied the patch in the thirty-four-day interval between public disclosure and the breach event.
45	
46	The attacker leveraged the unpatched vulnerability to gain access to production database systems containing UK patient records. The forensic investigation confirmed that data exfiltration occurred over a period of approximately seventy-two hours between 14 September and 17 September 2024. The following categories of personal data were affected:
47	
48	> • **Mental health treatment records:** 41,203 records, including diagnoses, treatment plans, and clinical notes --- constituting special category data under Article 9 of the UK GDPR;
49	>
50	> • **Prescription data records:** 87,614 records, including medication names, dosages, prescribing clinician details, and dispensing history;
51	>
52	> • **General medical records:** 183,600 records, including patient names, NHS numbers, dates of birth, medical diagnoses (ICD-10 codes), and clinical correspondence.
53	
54	In total, 312,417 UK patient records were affected. The compromised data fields included full patient names, NHS numbers, dates of birth, medical diagnoses, prescription histories, and, in the case of mental health records, detailed clinical treatment notes and referral information.
55	
56	BHS UK notified the ICO on 19 September 2024, within the seventy-two-hour statutory notification period under Article 33 of the UK GDPR. Data subject notifications were issued in phases between 25 September and 12 October 2024 in accordance with Article 34, with priority given to the 41,203 individuals whose mental health records were compromised. BHS UK also notified the affected NHS trusts and private clinic partners during this period.
57	
58	**2.2 The ICO Investigation**
59	
60	The ICO commenced its formal investigation into the breach on 2 October 2024 under Case Reference ICO/INV/2024/09871. The investigation was led by Deputy Commissioner Eleanor Voss and supported by a team from the ICO\'s Investigations Directorate. BHS UK cooperated fully with the investigation, providing documentary evidence, system access for technical review, and staff interviews as requested.
61	
62	The investigation identified fourteen specific failings across five domains: technical security measures (including patch management, encryption standards, and access controls), organisational measures (including staff training and governance structures), data protection impact assessment practices, data processor oversight, and breach response and notification procedures. The ICO\'s assessment concluded that these failings constituted infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 24, 25, 28, 32, 33, 34, and 35 of the UK GDPR.
63	
64	A Preliminary Enforcement Notice was issued on 18 November 2024, setting out the ICO\'s findings and indicating the potential for a formal monetary penalty notice. The maximum monetary penalty available to the ICO in this matter was assessed at up to GBP 8.7 million. This figure was derived from the ICO\'s assessment methodology, taking into account the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, the number of data subjects affected, and the degree of responsibility demonstrated by BHS UK. For reference, the statutory maximum penalty under Section 157 of the Data Protection Act 2018 is the higher of GBP 17.5 million or four per cent of total annual worldwide turnover; four per cent of BHS\'s global revenue of USD 485 million (approximately GBP 387 million at an exchange rate of 1.254) equates to approximately GBP 15.48 million. The ICO assessed the appropriate penalty at GBP 8.7 million based on the specific circumstances of the case.
65	
66	Following extensive engagement between BHS UK, Thornfield & Associates LLP, and the ICO, the parties agreed to a Regulatory Undertaking as an alternative to formal enforcement action. The Regulatory Undertaking was signed on 15 January 2025 by Jonathan Kierce, Managing Director of BHS UK, and Deputy Commissioner Eleanor Voss. The Undertaking contains forty-seven specific commitments across eight domains, with compliance to be achieved in four phases over a twelve-month period.

Certain Undertaking commitments have been subdivided into discrete implementation sub-actions where necessary for operational clarity and effective project management. Each action item specifies the corresponding Undertaking commitment, a detailed description of the required deliverable, the designated action owner, the allocated budget, the target completion date, and the evidence deliverables required for compliance verification.
89	
90	Implementation is structured across four phases aligned with the deadlines established in the Undertaking: Phase 1 (Critical --- by 14 February 2025), Phase 2 (High Priority --- by 15 April 2025), Phase 3 (Medium Priority --- by 14 July 2025), and Phase 4 (Completion --- by 15 January 2026). The Plan further establishes a comprehensive reporting structure, escalation mechanisms, and evidence-gathering protocols to ensure that all remediation activities are documented, auditable, and verifiable by both the appointed independent auditor and the ICO.

47	The ICO\'s investigation has established the following chronology of events relevant to the personal data breach that is the subject of this investigation:

CVE-2024-31742 was assigned a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (\"CVSS\") base score of 9.8 out of 10.0, classifying it as \"Critical.\" The vendor simultaneously released a security patch addressing the vulnerability on this date, and the disclosure was accompanied by advisories from the National Cyber Security Centre (\"NCSC\") and other authoritative bodies recommending immediate remediation.
50

The ICO\'s investigation found that the delay was attributable to the absence of any automated patch management system at BHS UK, with the organisation instead relying upon ad hoc manual patch assessment and deployment processes. 102	
103	The fourteen findings set out below relate primarily to alleged infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 24, 25, 28, 32, and 35 of the UK GDPR. The ICO has identified both technical and organisational failures of a systemic nature.
104	
105	**[5. Summary of Investigation Findings]{.underline}**
106	
107	The ICO\'s investigation has identified fourteen (14) specific findings, which are grouped thematically below under two categories: Technical Findings (Findings 1--5) and Organisational Findings (Findings 6--14). Each finding includes a description of the failing, a summary of the evidence relied upon, and the relevant UK GDPR provision(s) engaged.
108	
109	**Part A --- Technical Findings**
110	
111	**Finding 1 --- Failure to Implement Timely Patch Management**
112	
113	BHS UK failed to apply the vendor-supplied security patch for CVE-2024-31742 for a period of thirty-four (34) calendar days following its public disclosure on 14 August 2024, despite the vulnerability carrying a CVSS base score of 9.8 (Critical). The investigation established that BHS UK had no automated patch management system in place and instead relied upon ad hoc manual patch assessment and deployment processes that were neither documented nor subject to defined service-level commitments. No documented patch management policy was in effect at any time material to this investigation. The thirty-four-day remediation gap for a vulnerability of this severity, in a system processing special category health data at scale, constitutes a fundamental failure to implement appropriate technical measures under Article 32(1)(b) and (d) of the UK GDPR. The ICO considers this failing to be a direct and proximate cause of the breach.
114	
115	**Finding 2 --- Inadequate Encryption Practices**
116	
117	The investigation identified that personal data at rest in certain BellCloud UK data stores was encrypted using the AES-128 encryption standard rather than AES-256, which is the standard the ICO considers appropriate for data of this sensitivity and volume. Additionally, multiple data flows between BHS UK systems and NHS trust endpoints were found to be operating using TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, both of which are deprecated protocols known to contain exploitable vulnerabilities. Even where TLS 1.2 was in use, the ICO considers this insufficient given the sensitivity of the health data being transmitted; TLS 1.3 is the appropriate standard for all data flows involving special category health data of this nature. These failings constitute a breach of Article 32(1)(a) of the UK GDPR, which specifically references encryption as an appropriate technical measure.
118	
119	**Finding 3 --- Deficient Access Controls**
120	
121	BHS UK operated an insufficiently granular access control framework for the BellCloud UK environment. The investigation identified twenty-three (23) administrative accounts with unrestricted access to the patient data production environment, of which eight (8) belonged to individuals who had left the organisation and whose accounts had not been deactivated or revoked. No systematic access review process was in place. Multi-factor authentication (\"MFA\") was not enforced for privileged accounts accessing the patient data environment. These failings represent a breach of Article 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR, specifically the obligation to ensure the ongoing confidentiality and integrity of processing systems and services.
122	
123	**Finding 4 --- Insufficient Network Segmentation**
124	
125	The BellCloud UK architecture lacked adequate network segmentation. The investigation confirmed that the compromised API gateway component had direct, unsegmented network access to the production database containing all 312,417 patient records. No demilitarised zone, micro-segmentation, or other network isolation measures were in place to limit lateral movement within the production environment. Had proper network segmentation been implemented, the scope of the breach could reasonably have been limited. This constitutes a failure under Article 25 of the UK GDPR (data protection by design) and Article 32 (security of processing).
126	
127	**Finding 5 --- Absence of Regular Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Scanning**
128	
129	BHS UK had not conducted an external penetration test of the BellCloud UK platform for a period of fourteen (14) months prior to the date of the breach. No regular or scheduled vulnerability scanning programme was operational. Had such testing and scanning measures been in place and functioning, it is the ICO\'s assessment that CVE-2024-31742 would likely have been identified following its public disclosure and would have been prioritised for immediate remediation. The ICO notes the importance of penetration testing being conducted by an independent provider holding appropriate accreditation, such as CREST accreditation, to ensure the rigour and reliability of the testing. This failing constitutes a breach of Article 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR --- the obligation to implement a process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing.
130	
131	**Part B --- Organisational Findings**
132	
133	**Finding 6 --- Inadequate Data Protection Impact Assessments**
134	
135	BHS UK had not conducted any data protection impact assessment (\"DPIA\") for the BellCloud UK platform, despite that platform processing health data --- special category data under Article 9 of the UK GDPR --- at significant scale. No DPIA framework existed within the organisation. No DPIA register was maintained. No documented DPIA review triggers had been established. The processing of 312,417 health records, including 41,203 mental health treatment records, through a cloud-based platform accessible across multiple NHS trusts and private clinics, clearly constitutes high-risk processing requiring a DPIA under Article 35(1) and (3) of the UK GDPR. The ICO considers the absence of any DPIA for this processing activity to be a serious organisational failing.
136	
137	**Finding 7 --- Deficient Processor and Sub-Processor Oversight**
138	
139	BHS UK engages multiple third-party data processors and sub-processors for various elements of the BellCloud UK service. The investigation reviewed twelve (12) processor relationships and identified the following deficiencies: (a) Article 28 processor agreements were outdated, incomplete, or absent for seven (7) of the twelve (12) relationships reviewed; (b) no formal sub-processor due diligence programme existed --- sub-processors were engaged without any prior privacy risk assessment being conducted; (c) there was no contractual flow-down of Article 28 obligations to sub-processors engaged by BHS UK\'s processors; and (d) no systematic processor audit programme was in place, and no audits of processors or sub-processors had been conducted in the twenty-four (24) months preceding the breach. These failings constitute a breach of Article 28 of the UK GDPR. The ICO particularly emphasises the absence of any sub-processor due diligence programme as a discrete and significant failing.
140	
141	**Finding 8 --- Inadequate International Transfer Safeguards**
142	
143	BHS UK routinely transfers personal data, including the special category health data processed through BellCloud UK, to its parent company, BHS Inc., at its offices in Austin, Texas, United States of America. The investigation found that no Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\"), Binding Corporate Rules (\"BCRs\"), or other transfer mechanism compliant with Chapter V of the UK GDPR (Articles 44--49) was in place for this intra-group transfer. Additionally, no Transfer Risk Assessment (\"TRA\") had been conducted to assess the level of protection afforded to personal data in the United States. The ICO notes that the United States is not subject to a general UK adequacy decision for the purposes of the UK GDPR. While the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework may provide an appropriate basis for certain transfers, this mechanism must be specifically assessed and documented, and BHS UK had undertaken no such assessment. These failings constitute a breach of Articles 44 to 49 of the UK GDPR (Chapter V --- Transfers of Personal Data to Third Countries or International Organisations). The absence of any transfer safeguard for the routine transfer of sensitive health data to the US parent company is a matter of serious concern.
144	
145	**Finding 9 --- Insufficient Staff Training and Awareness**
146	
147	BHS UK had no mandatory annual data protection training programme in place. Of the 342 members of staff employed across BHS UK\'s London, Manchester, and Edinburgh offices, only 124 (approximately 36%) had received any form of data protection training in the twelve (12) months preceding the breach. No role-based specialist training programme existed for staff who handle sensitive or special category data as part of their duties. No phishing awareness programme had been implemented. Training records were incomplete, inconsistent, and unauditable. These failings constitute a breach of Article 24 of the UK GDPR (responsibility of the controller) and Article 32 (organisational measures), in that BHS UK failed to implement appropriate organisational measures --- including ensuring staff competence through qualified and externally delivered training --- to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risks of its processing activities.
148	
149	**Finding 10 --- Failure to Implement Data Minimisation and Retention Controls**
150	
151	BHS UK had no documented retention schedule for patient data processed through BellCloud UK. Data was retained indefinitely without review or purging. No automated deletion workflows were in place. No evidence of data minimisation reviews having been conducted was identified. Of particular concern, the investigation confirmed that special category data --- including mental health treatment records relating to 41,203 individuals --- was present in non-production environments, specifically test, development, staging, quality assurance (\"QA\"), analytics, and reporting environments, without pseudonymisation or any other appropriate safeguard. The ICO considers that 100% of special category data present in all non-production environments must be pseudonymised or otherwise appropriately protected. These failings constitute breaches of Article 5(1)(c) (data minimisation) and Article 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) of the UK GDPR.
152	
153	**Finding 11 --- Deficient Breach Response and Internal Escalation Procedures**
154	
155	While BHS UK\'s notification to the ICO within seventy-two (72) hours of discovery was compliant with Article 33 of the UK GDPR, the investigation identified significant and concerning weaknesses in BHS UK\'s internal breach response and escalation procedures. No documented incident response plan existed at the time of the breach. The DPO, Dr. Fiona Hartwell, was not notified of the breach until approximately thirty-six (36) hours after the IT Security team\'s initial discovery of anomalous activity on 17 September 2024 --- a delay the ICO considers unacceptable for an organisation processing special category data at this scale. There was no internal escalation service-level agreement (\"SLA\"), no tabletop breach simulation or exercise programme, and no post-incident review process. The ICO emphasises that BHS UK must implement a maximum twenty-four (24) hour internal escalation SLA from discovery of a potential personal data breach (whether confirmed or suspected) to notification of the DPO, ensuring the DPO is in a position to assess notification obligations promptly.
156	
157	**Finding 12 --- Inadequate DPO Reporting Line and Governance**
158	
159	The DPO, Dr. Fiona Hartwell, reported directly to BHS UK\'s Managing Director, Jonathan Kierce, who in turn reported to the General Counsel of BHS Inc., Priya Dasgupta, based in Austin, Texas. The DPO had no direct reporting line to the board of directors of Bellhaven Health UK Ltd. Article 38(3) of the UK GDPR requires that the DPO shall directly report to the highest management level of the controller. It is the ICO\'s position that, for BHS UK as a UK-incorporated entity, this means a direct reporting line to the board of directors of Bellhaven Health UK Ltd., without management intermediation through the Managing Director or through the General Counsel of the US parent company. The investigation also found that there was no quarterly data protection compliance reporting to the BHS UK board, no designated board-level privacy champion, and that the records of processing activities required under Article 30 of the UK GDPR were outdated and incomplete.
160	
161	**Finding 13 --- Inadequate Transparency and Data Subject Rights Processes**
162	
163	BHS UK\'s privacy notices were outdated, having last been updated in March 2021, and did not accurately describe the organisation\'s current processing activities or the full range of data subject rights available under the UK GDPR. The data subject access request (\"DSAR\") response process was entirely manual and had resulted in at least three (3) documented instances where DSARs were not responded to within the one calendar month period prescribed by Article 12(3) of the UK GDPR. No automated DSAR portal or case management system was in place. Additionally, no children\'s data assessment had been conducted despite BHS UK processing personal data relating to patients under the age of eighteen (18). An estimated 28,000 records within BellCloud UK relate to individuals aged under 18. No assessment against the ICO\'s Age-Appropriate Design Code (\"AADC\") had been carried out. The ICO considers the absence of any children\'s data assessment and AADC compliance review to be a distinct and material gap in BHS UK\'s compliance posture.
164	
165	**Finding 14 --- Absence of Privacy-by-Design Framework**
166	
167	BHS UK had no documented privacy-by-design framework in place at any time material to this investigation. New processing activities and system changes were implemented without any systematic or structured consideration of data protection requirements at the design stage. The BellCloud UK platform underwent two major version upgrades in the twelve (12) months preceding the breach, neither of which included a privacy impact assessment or any form of privacy-by-design review. This constitutes a failure under Article 25 of the UK GDPR, which requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles in an effective manner and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing, both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself.
168	
169	**[6. Severity Assessment]{.underline}**
170	
171	The ICO has assessed the overall severity of the failings identified in this investigation and considers them to be serious within the meaning of the ICO\'s Regulatory Action Policy, for the following reasons:
172	
173	**Scale of the Breach.** The personal data breach affected 312,417 individuals --- a significant number by any measure, and particularly so in the context of health data processed on behalf of NHS trusts and private healthcare providers.
174	
175	**Sensitivity of the Data.** The data compromised in the breach included special category data (health data) within the meaning of Article 9 of the UK GDPR. Within that dataset, 41,203 records contained highly sensitive mental health treatment records. The unauthorised disclosure of mental health data carries an exceptionally high risk of harm to affected individuals, including risks of stigmatisation, discrimination, distress, and reputational damage.
176	
177	**Proximate Cause.** The thirty-four-day failure to patch a publicly known critical vulnerability (CVE-2024-31742, CVSS 9.8) in the BellCloud UK API gateway represents a fundamental and proximate failure in technical security measures. The patch was available from the date of public disclosure. The delay was entirely avoidable.
178	
179	**Systemic Nature of Failings.** The breadth of organisational failings identified --- spanning data protection impact assessments, processor and sub-processor management, staff training, governance, transparency, data minimisation, breach response, international transfers, and privacy-by-design --- indicates systemic rather than isolated failures in BHS UK\'s compliance programme. These are not the hallmarks of a single operational lapse but of an organisation that had not invested adequately in data protection infrastructure commensurate with the volume and sensitivity of the data it processes.
180	
181	**Potential Monetary Penalty.** The ICO notes that, under Article 83(5) of the UK GDPR and section 157 of the DPA 2018, the ICO may impose a penalty of up to the higher of £17.5 million or 4% of total annual worldwide turnover of the undertaking concerned. For BHS Inc. (as the relevant undertaking), 4% of total annual worldwide turnover equates to up to approximately £15.48 million (calculated as 4% of approximately £387 million). The ICO\'s initial assessment, taking into account mitigating factors --- including BHS UK\'s timely notification of the breach to the ICO, its cooperation throughout the investigation, and its proactive engagement of Ridgeline Cybersecurity Consultants Ltd. for forensic analysis and remediation support --- places the potential monetary penalty at up to £8.7 million. This figure represents the ICO\'s preliminary view and is subject to revision in light of BHS UK\'s response to the Preliminary Enforcement Notice and any subsequent regulatory undertaking.
182	
183	**[7. Next Steps and Regulatory Undertaking Pathway]{.underline}**
184	
185	The Preliminary Enforcement Notice issued on this date, 18 November 2024, sets out the ICO\'s intention to take regulatory action against BHS UK in respect of the infringements identified in the fourteen findings summarised above. BHS UK has the right to make written representations to the ICO in response to the Preliminary Enforcement Notice within twenty-eight (28) calendar days of the date of service of that notice --- that is, by no later than 16 December 2024.
186	
187	The ICO indicates its willingness to consider a regulatory undertaking under section 155 of the DPA 2018 as an alternative to formal enforcement action, provided that BHS UK commits to a comprehensive and verifiable programme of remediation that addresses all fourteen findings across eight (8) defined domains. The ICO expects that any regulatory undertaking must address each of the following domains:
188	
189	> 1\. **Technical Security Measures** --- addressing Findings 1 through 5, encompassing patch management, encryption, access controls, network segmentation, penetration testing, vulnerability scanning, logging and monitoring, and multi-factor authentication;
190	>
191	> 2\. **Data Protection Impact Assessments** --- addressing Finding 6, encompassing a DPIA framework, retrospective DPIAs for existing high-risk processing, DPIA review triggers, an ICO consultation threshold mechanism, and a DPIA register;
192	>
193	> 3\. **Data Processor Management** --- addressing Finding 7, encompassing Article 28 agreement remediation, sub-processor due diligence, contractual flow-downs, processor audits, and ongoing processor risk assessments;
194	>
195	> 4\. **Staff Training and Awareness** --- addressing Finding 9, encompassing mandatory annual training, role-based specialist training, phishing awareness, and auditable training records;
196	>
197	> 5\. **Data Minimisation and Retention** --- addressing Finding 10, encompassing retention schedules, automated deletion workflows, data minimisation reviews, and pseudonymisation of special category data in all non-production environments;
198	>
199	> 6\. **Breach Response and Notification** --- addressing Finding 11, encompassing a documented incident response plan, internal escalation SLAs, tabletop exercises, post-incident reviews, breach notification templates, and breach registers;
200	>
201	> 7\. **Governance and Accountability** --- addressing Findings 12 and 14, encompassing DPO reporting lines, board-level privacy governance, Article 30 records, privacy-by-design frameworks, and privacy impact assessments for system changes; and
202	>
203	> 8\. **Transparency and Data Subject Rights** --- addressing Findings 8 and 13, encompassing privacy notice updates, DSAR processes, children\'s data assessments, AADC compliance reviews, and international transfer safeguards.
204	
205	Any regulatory undertaking agreed between the ICO and BHS UK will be required to include: phased implementation with clearly defined deadlines for each commitment; quarterly progress reporting to the ICO on a schedule to be agreed; independent audit by an ICO-approved auditor covering all remediation areas; and auditable evidence chains for all remediation activities.
206

uction environments. That puts us at 28 February at the earliest, realistical=

To give you the full picture: the deployment involves 47 NHS trust-facing API=
 endpoints and 218 private clinic connections. We can't just flip a switch. E=
ach integration point needs validation, and we've learned the hard way on oth=
er engagements that rushing this creates more vulnerabilities than it fixes.

as implement interim manual patching processes across the estate. That's been=

atching cycle for critical CVEs through manual processes. But I want to be ho=

t's a bridging measure.

g process as a mitigating measure while the automated system comes online. Th=
at way, if anyone asks what's been happening between signing and full deploym=
ent, the answer isn't "nothing" =E2=80=94 it's "we've been patching manually =
to a near-compliant cycle and the automated platform is in procurement."

**TLS 1.3**

Several NHS trusts flatly refuse TLS 1.3 upgrade. We've tested against all 47=
 trust environments, and 11 of them are running gateway appliances that only =
support up to TLS 1.2. Three of those trusts handle mental health data =E2=80=
=94 roughly 12,000 of the 41,203 special category records.

are replacement at the trust end to support TLS 1.3. That's outside BHS's con=
trol entirely.

 data feeds to 11 NHS trusts. That's not an option =E2=80=94 patient safety c=

ymising them would require a separate data masking layer that doesn't current=

eudonymisation rules on the fly.

essed by a smaller team with existing role-based access controls and audit lo=
